5Extend it

Tools, MCP, skills: new abilities without a new model.

ⓘ Notes
Tools give it new actions, MCP plugs in tools others built, and skills give it know-how loaded on demand. All their descriptions take context.

Why it’s designed this way: Changing the model is slow and costly; manuals and hands from outside work the same day.

② Diagram

What a model knows is fixed at training time. The cheapest way to make it do new things is to hand it manuals and hands from outside. Three ways:

  • Tools (function calling): give it a new action (check stock, send a message).
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol): plug in whole sets of tools and data others have built, through one open protocol.
  • Skills (skill packs): hand it a pack of “how to do this kind of task” instructions (scripts optional), read only when needed.

All three share one cost: their descriptions must go into the Context window before the model knows they exist.

③ Details · why

A tool is two things a developer writes: a manual for the model (name, purpose, parameter format) and the program that does the work. For example: Illustrative

{
  "name": "check_stock",
  "description": "Look up the stock count of a product",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": { "sku": { "type": "string" } },
    "required": ["sku"]
  }
}

When needed, the model writes text like {"name":"check_stock","arguments":{"sku":"A-102"}}; the program checks the arguments, calls the real system and sends the result back as text. Details in Tool manual (function description) and ⑤ Tool result.

Good tools: obvious names, a description that says when to use it, few parameters; keep read-only tools apart from ones that change things, and add confirmation to the latter.

③ Details · why

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol proposed in late 2024. Before it, each AI app had to integrate each tool separately (N apps × M tools); with one protocol, each side implements it once and they connect (N + M).

  • Three roles: the AI app (host) (the AI app you use) opens one MCP client per server, connected to an MCP server.
  • A server offers three kinds of things: tools (actions), resources (data to read) and prompts (ready-made templates).
  • Two ways to connect: standard input/output (stdio) when the server runs locally; HTTP when it is remote.

Safety: installing a server means trusting its code and everything it can reach, and what it returns may carry a Prompt injection. Install only trusted ones, and check the access they ask for.

③ Details · why

A skill is a folder: a SKILL.md file says how to do a kind of task, starting with a name and a one-line description; it may also hold scripts and templates.

  1. Normally: only each skill’s name and description sit in the context, a few dozen tokens each.
  2. When relevant: the agent decides a skill fits the task, then reads the full instructions and runs its scripts if needed.

🧪 How much context do the manuals take?

ⓘ All token counts are illustrative round numbers; real ones depend on the model and how descriptions are written.

Why it’s built this way:
  • Every extension must introduce itself first, in the context; the more you install, the more crowded it gets.
  • Loading on demand (name and one line first, full text when used) is how skills and many tool systems save room.



👀 Try this:
  • Pick 30, put everything in, and see how much the manuals take
  • Switch to “load on demand” and compare
  • With on-demand loading, tap “Call a tool once” and see when the full manual comes in
